hooks.command: cd "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR" && git add -A && git diff --cached --quiet || { git commit -q -m "auto: update via Claude Code" -m "Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>" && git push -q origin HEAD; }

hooks.prompt: This edit was just auto-committed and pushed to origin/main by this repo's PostToolUse hook (no manual `firebase deploy` step is used anymore — a push to main is what triggers the GitHub Actions deploy to Firebase Hosting). Start by looking at exactly what changed in THIS commit — run `git show --stat HEAD` then `git diff HEAD~1 HEAD -- . ':!CLAUDE.md'` — and use that diff as your PRIMARY signal, reading only as much surrounding code as needed to understand it. Do not re-diff the whole codebase against all of CLAUDE.md from scratch each time; that is expensive and biases toward missing things. Update CLAUDE.md if this diff is doc-worthy. 'Doc-worthy' includes not just new commands/architecture/top-level files/a bumped service-worker cache version, but also real logic or behavior changes to a function CLAUDE.md already describes: an added/removed/changed parameter, a changed call signature, changed control flow, or a changed data shape (fields added/removed/renamed on an object the function reads or writes). If CLAUDE.md's description of a touched function or flow is now inaccurate or incomplete because of this diff, fix it. Only edit CLAUDE.md if something in this diff is actually doc-worthy; otherwise do nothing and exit quietly. If the diff alone lacks context (e.g. it's one step of a larger multi-step feature), you may check `git log --oneline -5` or skim the touched file's relevant section — but keep the investigation scoped to what this diff touched, not a full repo re-scan.
